title: Post-incident summary examples (good/bad) + annotations
content:
Purpose
This doc is for training Incident Commanders (ICs) and Comms Leads on writing publishable post-incident summaries for the public Status Page.

It includes:
- “Good” examples that meet our standards (clarity, accuracy, fast-to-publish, no sensitive disclosures)
- “Bad” examples that look plausible internally but should NOT be published as-is
- Annotations explaining what to copy, what to avoid, and why

Audience
- SRE on-call (IC/Scribe/Comms Lead)
- Support/CS leads who review language for customer impact framing
- Legal/Security reviewers for high-severity events

Publishing constraints (quick checklist)
1) Say what customers need to know: impact, timeframe, affected components/regions, and current state.
2) Avoid sensitive details:
   - Don’t name specific customers, quotas, contracts, or “we ran out of capacity for Customer X.”
   - Don’t disclose exploitable infrastructure details (exact GPU counts, vendor incident tickets, internal hostnames, non-public regions).
   - Don’t imply new SLAs or refunds (“we guarantee…”, “we will credit…”) unless approved.
3) Be precise about uncertainty:
   - If root cause is not fully confirmed, use “We believe…”, “Preliminary analysis indicates…”, “We are continuing to validate…”
4) Use consistent taxonomy:
   - Component names should match the status page component list and region naming.
5) Match internal signals:
   - Don’t declare “fully resolved” while dashboards show ongoing elevated errors/latency.

Recommended structure (what ‘good’ looks like)
- Summary (1–2 sentences)
- Customer impact (what failed and who was affected; avoid marketing language)
- Timeline (all times in UTC; 4–8 bullets is usually enough)
- Root cause (one paragraph; include “class” of failure; don’t over-speculate)
- Mitigation & recovery (what we did; what customers could do, if applicable)
- Preventing recurrence (3–6 follow-ups; concrete, testable; include owners if internal-only)

============================================================
EXAMPLE A — GOOD (publishable): US-East streaming degradation
Incident: Partial streaming degradation in us-east
Components: Hosted API > Streaming (us-east)
Severity: Sev1

Public post-incident summary (example)
Summary
On 2025-11-07, we experienced degraded streaming responses for a subset of Hosted API requests in the us-east region. Affected customers saw elevated streaming disconnects and intermittent token delivery stalls. The issue was mitigated and service recovered.

Customer impact
- Impacted capability: Streaming responses (Hosted API)
- Impacted region: us-east
- Symptoms observed: elevated disconnects, stalled streams requiring retry; non-streaming requests were largely unaffected
- Time window: 2025-11-07 18:12–18:47 UTC (intermittent residual recovery through ~19:05 UTC)

Timeline (UTC)
- 18:12 — Monitoring detected increased streaming disconnect rate in us-east.
- 18:16 — Incident declared; investigation started.
- 18:21 — Identified correlation with a subset of streaming gateway instances.
- 18:28 — Mitigation applied (traffic shifted away from the affected pool; connection handling settings adjusted).
- 18:35 — Error rates and disconnects began returning to baseline.
- 18:47 — Service considered recovered; continued monitoring.
- 19:05 — Confirmed sustained stability on streaming health dashboards.

Root cause
A configuration change in the us-east streaming gateway tier interacted with a connection-handling edge case under load, increasing the likelihood of disconnects for long-lived streaming sessions.

Mitigation and recovery
We shifted traffic away from the affected gateway pool and adjusted connection-handling parameters to reduce disconnect likelihood. Customers who encountered stalled streams were able to recover by retrying the request.

Preventing recurrence
- Add region-aware streaming disconnect metrics and alerts for earlier detection and component-level visibility.
- Expand canary coverage for streaming configuration changes, including long-lived session tests.
- Add automated rollback triggers when streaming disconnect rate crosses threshold.

Annotations (why this is good)
- Uses correct component + region language (“Hosted API > Streaming (us-east)”).
- Clear customer symptoms without implying data loss or other unconfirmed harms.
- Timeline is concise and in UTC.
- Root cause is explained at the right level: mechanism/class, not internal hostnames or vendor blame.
- Includes concrete follow-ups without listing private implementation details.

What to copy/paste from this example
- The impact bullets (“capability, region, symptoms, time window”).
- The timeline density (not every internal action; only customer-relevant milestones).

============================================================
EXAMPLE B — BAD (not publishable): Same incident, overly vague + inconsistent + missing facts
Draft (bad example)
We had some issues with the API today in the East region. Some customers may have had trouble. The team is looking into it and we believe it’s fixed now. We will make sure this doesn’t happen again.

Annotations (what’s wrong)
- “Some issues” and “some customers” are too vague to be actionable.
- Doesn’t name the affected capability (Streaming vs non-streaming matters materially).
- “We believe it’s fixed now” without any time window or confirmation criteria.
- No timeline; customers can’t correlate logs.
- “We will make sure this doesn’t happen again” over-promises and reads like an SLA guarantee.

How to rewrite quickly
- Replace “API issues” with exact component (“Hosted API > Streaming (us-east)”).
- Add a time window and symptoms.
- Add 4–6 timeline bullets and a one-paragraph root cause class.

============================================================
EXAMPLE C — GOOD (publishable): Embeddings elevated 5xx due to misclassification + rollback
Incident: Elevated 5xx for Embeddings requests across eu-west
Components: Hosted API > Embeddings (eu-west)
Severity: Sev2

Public post-incident summary (example)
Summary
On 2025-11-18, we experienced elevated error rates for Embeddings requests in the eu-west region. The issue was caused by an incorrect request classification introduced in a deployment and was resolved by rolling back the change.

Customer impact
- Impacted capability: Embeddings
- Impacted region: eu-west
- Symptoms observed: elevated HTTP 5xx responses for a subset of Embeddings requests
- Time window: 2025-11-18 09:44–10:13 UTC

Timeline (UTC)
- 09:44 — Error rate alert triggered for Embeddings in eu-west.
- 09:48 — Incident declared; investigation began.
- 09:56 — Identified recent deployment correlated with error increase.
- 10:02 — Rolled back the deployment.
- 10:08 — Error rates returned to baseline.
- 10:13 — Incident resolved after confirming stability.

Root cause
A deployment introduced an incorrect classification for a subset of Embeddings requests, causing them to be routed through an incompatible handling path and resulting in increased server errors.

Mitigation and recovery
We rolled back the deployment and verified recovery via Embeddings error-rate and latency dashboards.

Preventing recurrence
- Add validation tests for request classification to CI.
- Expand monitoring to detect mismatches between route tags and component mapping.
- Improve rollout safeguards for routing/classification changes.

Annotations (why this is good)
- Names “Embeddings” explicitly; avoids lumping under “API.”
- Root cause is understandable but not sensitive.
- Mentions the mitigation (rollback) clearly and ties resolution to verification.

============================================================
EXAMPLE D — BAD (not publishable): Leaks sensitive capacity + customer info
Draft (bad example)
We ran out of A100 capacity in us-east after Customer ABC’s workload spiked and preempted the shared pool. This caused streaming to drop for other tenants. We moved them to a dedicated cluster and added 64 more GPUs.

Annotations (what’s wrong)
- Names a customer (never publish).
- Discloses internal hardware type and counts (not appropriate for public summaries).
- Reveals multi-tenant dynamics in a way that can create reputational/security risk.
- Implies a commercial action (“moved them to a dedicated cluster”) that may not be universally true and is not necessary for customers to understand.

Safer rewrite pattern
- “Capacity constraints in a regional pool contributed to elevated errors for a subset of requests.”
- Focus on customer symptoms and what we did operationally at a high level (“shifted traffic, increased headroom, improved autoscaling safeguards”).

============================================================
EXAMPLE E — BORDERLINE (needs edits): Too much internal process, not enough customer impact
Draft (needs work)
At 03:12 UTC we spun up an incident Zoom, assigned IC, Comms Lead, and Scribe, and opened an internal ticket. At 03:20 we checked the dashboards and agreed it was Sev1. At 03:23 we contacted the runtime team.

Annotations
- Internal process is fine, but customers don’t need step-by-step of our coordination.
- Missing the actual impact, affected components, and how customers were affected.

How to fix
- Keep 1 timeline bullet for “incident declared” and replace the rest with technical/customer-relevant milestones (detected, identified, mitigated, recovered).

============================================================
Dedicated / Private notes (special handling)
- Dedicated: If impact was isolated to a single customer’s dedicated cluster, do not publish customer-identifying details. Status page language should be scoped appropriately (e.g., “Dedicated Control Plane” vs “Hosted API”) per current policy. When in doubt, involve Support lead + Legal for Sev0/Sev1.
- Private (VPC/on-prem): Avoid publishing architecture specifics or anything that reveals customer network design. If a public update is required, keep it at the platform/control-plane component level and confirm approval chain.

Copy blocks (safe phrasing)
- Uncertainty: “We are continuing to investigate the underlying cause. We will share additional details as they are confirmed.”
- Partial impact: “A subset of requests in <region> experienced elevated errors/latency.”
- Mitigation: “We mitigated the issue by shifting traffic and applying configuration changes. Service has returned to normal operation.”
- Verification: “We confirmed recovery by monitoring error rate and latency returning to baseline on component health dashboards.”

Avoid these phrases
- “We guarantee…” / “This will never happen again…”
- “All customers were impacted” (unless verified)
- “No customer data was impacted” (unless you are explicitly authorized to make that claim; usually avoid unless confirmed and necessary)

Review/approval reminders
- Sev0/Sev1: route draft through IC + Comms Lead + Support lead; escalate to Legal/Security reviewer if there’s any chance of sensitive disclosure.
- If the summary references Dedicated/Private, loop in Kira Thompson for guidance.

Notes to self (Wei)
- Once ENG-4823 auto-draft is live, update this doc to include an example of “good auto-generated draft” + the minimal manual edits required before publish.
- Add one example of “latency-only degradation” wording after we finalize criteria for ‘Degraded Performance’ vs ‘Partial Outage’ in the status signals standard.
